name: Tart cherry juice

lead: Tart cherry juice comes from sour cherries, most often the Montmorency cultivar, sold as juice or concentrate. People drink it for exercise recovery and as a food source of melatonin before bed, aiming for less soreness, more training and a more rested appearance.

Proponents point to melatonin and anthocyanin antioxidants. A randomized crossover study of 20 volunteers examined whether a concentrate raised urinary melatonin and improved sleep, a pilot study looked at older adults with insomnia, and other trials measured muscle damage and soreness. Studies are small.

paras: It is drunk as juice or mixed from concentrate, usually in the evening or around hard training, as part of a recovery routine. Users judge it over days to weeks.
It is a food product with sugar content. The sources reviewed give little data on adverse effects.

angle.text: Users drink tart cherry juice for exercise recovery and as a melatonin source for sleep, supporting training and a rested look. Small trials have measured sleep, soreness and muscle-damage markers; appearance effects have not been studied.

lead: Tart cherry juice is juice from sour cherries (Prunus cerasus), most commonly the Montmorency cultivar, grown largely in Michigan.[1] People drink it, or take it as a concentrate, to support recovery after hard training and to help sleep. Both goals feed into appearance: faster recovery from muscle soreness means more consistent training and so more muscle and a better physique over time, and better sleep is widely discussed as supporting skin, energy and training capacity.

Interest in the juice for sleep rests on the observation that Montmorency cherries contain phytochemicals including melatonin, the hormone that helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of 20 volunteers measured urinary melatonin and sleep after 7 days of a juice concentrate, and its authors concluded that the concentrate raised exogenous melatonin and was associated with improved sleep duration and quality.[2] A pilot crossover study of a proprietary cherry juice blend in older adults with insomnia examined subjective sleep reports.[3]

For recovery, the juice's anthocyanin pigments and other polyphenols are described as antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compounds. Trials in marathon runners, college students performing eccentric exercise and runners have measured muscle damage markers, strength loss and soreness.[4][5][6] A literature review in a sports-medicine journal summarised that tart cherry may lessen pain and speed strength recovery, and suggested it may be most relevant when recovery rather than adaptation is the priority.[7]

Tart cherry juice has a visible commercial and sports-nutrition culture around it. Cherry-industry sponsored content describes the juice as having a devoted following among professional athletes and recreational exercisers [8], researchers who have published on it describe faster recovery of muscle function after strenuous exercise as the most consistent finding [9], and independent trials in some sports, such as water polo and professional soccer, have reported no difference from placebo [10][11].
infobox: Bottled juice, concentrate, freeze-dried powder and capsules [12]

Sold as a food or dietary supplement

paras: The juice is tart and deep red because of anthocyanin pigments, and is sold as bottled juice, concentrate, freeze-dried powder and capsules.[1][12] Cherry juice in general is made by pressing cherries, filtering and usually pasteurising the liquid; hot extraction gives a deeper colour while cold extraction keeps a flavour closer to fresh cherries, and beverage versions are often diluted, sweetened or carbonated.[12] Montmorency is the best-known sour variety in the United States, and Balaton cherries are another sour variety used in studies.[1] Wikipedia lists U.S. production mainly in Wisconsin, with smaller amounts in other states, while Grokipedia names Michigan as a leading growing region.[1][12]

Wikipedia's nutrition figures give roughly 159 calories and 33 g of sugars per cup (about 240 mL) of cherry juice, with potassium and thiamine contributing meaningfully to daily values.[12] Cherry juice has a long food history: Wikipedia notes that Herodotus mentioned a people who drank it and that the ancient Romans did too.[12]

Its profile in sport rose in the 2000s as research groups published trials on cherries and exercise-induced muscle damage and on sleep, and sports-nutrition reviews began including it among recovery aids.[1][5][13] Retail products now range from single-strength juice to concentrates diluted in water, and from recovery drinks to bars, chews and gummies marketed with Montmorency cherries.[8]

Glyn Howatson, a sports scientist who co-authored several of the trials, traces the work to about 2006, when Connolly and McHugh at the University of Vermont reported that in an isolated muscle-damage model tart cherry juice sped recovery of muscle function and reduced soreness compared with placebo.[5][9] He describes later studies from UK and US laboratories reporting a benefit on at least one outcome after eccentric damage, marathon running, cycling, repeated-day exercise and team sports, with mixed results for inflammation and oxidative stress that he attributes to differences in exercise type and intensity.[9]

Howatson's summary is that the most consistent finding is faster recovery of muscle function in the days after hard exercise, and that the positive response is seen only with Montmorency tart cherries rather than cherries in general.[9] He is a co-author of some of the cited studies, and his site sells courses and products. Sleep research followed from the observation that the fruit contains melatonin, leading to the 2010 pilot in older adults with insomnia and the 2012 crossover study of urinary melatonin and sleep.[2][3]

Athletes in running, team sports and gym training drink the juice in the days around a hard session or event. The sports-medicine review notes that studies have commonly used a multi-day lead-in before an event and continued for a few days afterwards, and that the juice may be less suited to the adaptation phase of training, where some inflammation is part of the training signal.[7]

A 2018 review of supplements for athletes lists tart cherry among the products investigated for recovery.[13] A 2020 meta-analysis examined whether tart cherry concentrate changes endurance performance tests in healthy participants, noting that evidence for acute endurance benefits had been scarce.[14]

Howatson suggests that because the main compounds peak in the blood within a few hours of intake and fall back within roughly eight hours, multi-day loading used in early studies may not be necessary, and he proposes servings after exercise until soreness resolves; he describes this as reasoning from pharmacokinetics rather than a tested protocol.[9] Sponsored industry content describes products such as single-serve recovery beverages built around Montmorency cherries.[8]

People take the juice in the evening because of its reported melatonin content. Narrative reviews of nutrition and sleep list tart cherry juice among foods and nutrients that have been shown in some studies to improve aspects of sleep, alongside melatonin, tryptophan-rich protein and kiwifruit.[15][16] A 2022 randomised trial in elite female field hockey players examined Montmorency juice and sleep quality after intermittent exercise.[17]

A 2012 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in 20 healthy volunteers gave a tart cherry juice concentrate or placebo for 7 days, and measured sleep by actigraphy and questionnaires and urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin over 48 hours. Total melatonin content was reported as elevated, and the authors concluded the concentrate increased melatonin intake and was beneficial for sleep duration and quality.[2]

A 2010 pilot study in older adults with insomnia used a randomised, double-blind crossover design: each participant received a proprietary cherry juice blend and a placebo beverage for 2 weeks each, with a 2-week washout between them, and sleep continuity measures such as sleep onset, wake after sleep onset and total sleep time were examined.[3] A further 20-person pilot in older adults with insomnia, focused on feasibility and mechanisms, was registered in 2025.[18]

In a 2010 study, 20 recreational marathon runners took tart cherry juice or placebo for 5 days before, the day of and 48 hours after a marathon, with markers of muscle damage (creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, soreness, isometric strength), inflammation (IL-6, CRP, uric acid) and oxidative status measured.[4]

A 2006 randomised, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 14 male college students gave 12 fl oz of a cherry juice blend or placebo twice daily for eight days around a bout of eccentric elbow flexion contractions, testing whether it prevented the symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage.[5] A 2010 randomised trial examined muscle pain during running.[6]

Results are not uniform across studies. A 2020 trial in professional soccer players reported no effect of tart cherry juice on muscle function loss or muscle soreness after a match.[10] A 2024 randomised trial compared the juice with a sports drink on cycling performance, substrate metabolism and recovery,[19] and a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled trials on recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in athletes.[20]

A randomised, double-blind crossover trial of six days of tart cherry juice or placebo in nine well-trained water polo athletes reported no differences in any performance or recovery measure, and the authors suggested the intermittent, non-weight-bearing demands of the sport may not produce enough inflammation or oxidative stress for the juice to make a difference.[11] Sponsored coverage cites a UK study of 20 female dancers that found less self-reported soreness without differences in other muscle function measures, and a small cyclist study that reported improved 15 km time-trial performance, with two participants describing the gain as minimal.[8]

A 2009 trial reported that the juice decreased oxidative stress in healthy older men and women,[21] and a 2018 randomised crossover pilot study examined inflammation markers in overweight and obese subjects.[22] A pharmacokinetic study in people with a history of gout quantified the main anthocyanin in a juice concentrate.[23] Registered trials also address paclitaxel-induced neuropathy.[24]

Researchers attribute the juice's proposed effects to two groups of compounds. Anthocyanins such as cyanidin-3-glucosylrutinoside are antioxidant and anti-inflammatory polyphenols, and their absorption has been characterised in humans.[23] Melatonin is the other candidate: the 2012 study measured its main urinary metabolite and interpreted rises as evidence of exogenous melatonin from the juice.[2]

Tart cherry juice is sold as a food. It contains sugar, so concentrate and juice contribute calories and carbohydrate, and products differ between single-strength juice and concentrates. Published trials above reported results on recovery and sleep markers rather than a defined adverse-effect profile, and people with specific medical conditions or on medication commonly consult a clinician about supplements in general.

Tart cherry juice appears in recovery and sleep routines alongside magnesium, glycine and similar items, and in bodybuilding and endurance circles as a food-based recovery aid. On T Nation, lifters list it in training-log diets, for example 10 oz of tart cherry juice pre-workout alongside coffee, magnesium and a whey shake,[25] and one member notes that beet juice and tart cherry juice are big in the running and endurance world.[26]

It is typically discussed as a low-risk addition for people trying to train more often and sleep better, with appearance benefits understood as downstream of those goals. Wikipedia states that claims that it improves sleep in people with insomnia lack good evidence, while narrative nutrition reviews list it among foods studied for sleep.[12][15][16]

Much of the popular coverage of tart cherry juice for athletes is produced by growers, processors and brands. A search of coverage turns up sponsored articles for Montmorency cherries, promotional pieces citing sleep gains, and brand-ambassador arrangements with athletes, and one 2022 trade article carries a cherry-industry sponsored-content path.[8] Researchers and reviewers themselves describe the clinical evidence as small studies with mixed outcomes by sport and marker.[7][9]

lore.intro: In fitness and lifting communities tart cherry juice is mentioned as a recovery and sleep add-on and appears in training-log diets, with most detailed claims coming from sports scientists and sponsored industry content rather than looksmaxxing forums.[25][9][8]

claims.claim: It speeds recovery from hard training so you can train more.
Only Montmorency tart cherries work, not other cherries.
It improves sleep through its melatonin content.
A multi-day loading phase is needed before an event.
It is best for recovery periods, not for building adaptations.
Its anthocyanins lower inflammation and oxidative stress.
